requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'EvoPrompting: Language Models for Code-Level Neural Architecture Search' have been reproduced, including the evolutionary meta-learning algorithm with prompt-tuning, MNIST-1D convolutional architecture search, and CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark GNN search that produces novel triplet-representation architectures outperforming the Triplet-GMPNN baseline.

sub_tasks.requirements: The compute environment, ML frameworks (JAX, Flax, Haiku), optimizer (AdamW), and required hardware/library stack for running EvoPrompting on MNIST-1D and CLRS have been set up.
Python project scaffolding declares the deterministic dependency stack the paper relies on for both MNIST-1D (Flax) and CLRS (Haiku) child models.

Code has been implemented to declare project dependencies (in requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, environment.yml, or equivalent) that include JAX, Flax, dm-haiku, optax, and numpy so that both the MNIST-1D and CLRS pipelines can import their frameworks.
Code has been implemented to pin/record specific versions (or a lockfile) for JAX, Flax, dm-haiku, and optax so that runs are reproducible across attempts.
A top-level `reproduce.sh` (or equivalent single entrypoint) is present that installs dependencies and launches both the MNIST-1D and CLRS EvoPrompting experiments end-to-end.
The JAX / Flax / Haiku frameworks used to define, train, and evaluate child models can be imported and instantiated end-to-end.

Code has been implemented such that `import jax` and `import jax.numpy as jnp` succeed and a simple JIT-compiled function (e.g., matmul) executes and returns the correct value, confirming JAX is functional in the environment.

Code has been implemented so that `import flax` and `flax.linen as nn` succeed and a trivial `nn.Module` with `nn.Dense` can be instantiated and initialized, matching the framework used for the MNIST-1D seed models (Listings 2-5).

Code has been implemented so that `import haiku as hk` succeeds and an `hk.Linear` inside a transformed function can be initialized and applied, matching the framework used for the CLRS Triplet-GMPNN seed models (Appendix A.5).
The AdamW optimizer used to train every child model (Section 4.1 and 4.2) is available and behaves as an AdamW update step.

Code has been implemented that exposes an AdamW optimizer (e.g., via `optax.adamw`) wired into the child-model training loops for both MNIST-1D and CLRS, rather than falling back to plain Adam or SGD.

A unit test verifies that a single AdamW update step on a toy 1-D quadratic loss moves the parameter in the correct direction and applies decoupled weight decay (parameter magnitude shrinks under nonzero decay with zero gradient), confirming the optimizer implementation matches Loshchilov & Hutter (2019).
The compute environment provides the GPU acceleration and deterministic seeding the paper's per-child training loops depend on.

Code has been implemented that detects and uses a single CUDA GPU device via JAX (e.g., `jax.devices('gpu')`), consistent with the paper's use of one NVIDIA Tesla P100 per child model; if no P100 is available a functionally equivalent single-GPU device is used and this substitution is recorded in the results log.

Code has been implemented that centrally manages `jax.random.PRNGKey` seeding for model initialization, data shuffling, and mixed-temperature LM sampling, so that reruns with the same seed reproduce identical child model initializations.
The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark package and its assets (needed to define the Triplet-GMPNN processor the search modifies) are installable and importable within the environment.

Code has been implemented to install and import the `clrs` benchmark package (Veličković et al. 2022) as a dependency, so that dataset samplers and the Triplet-GMPNN processor scaffolding required by Section 4.2 are available at runtime.

The 62B-parameter PaLM code-fine-tuned language model used as the crossover/mutation operator is available (or a documented substitute is set up), configured for mixed-temperature sampling from {0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0}.
The backbone language model pi_theta_0 (62B PaLM code-fine-tuned, or a documented substitute) is acquired/configured and callable as the crossover/mutation operator.

Code has been implemented that loads or initializes a language model backbone corresponding to a 62B-parameter PaLM code-fine-tuned model (per Chowdhery et al. 2022), or documents and loads an explicit substitute (with model name and provider recorded in configuration/README).

Code has been implemented that documents the backbone's pre-training corpus attribution (1.3T tokens conversational/web/code, further fine-tuned on ~64B tokens of near-deduplicated permissively-licensed Python source) in configuration comments or README, matching Section 4's description.

Code has been implemented that exposes a callable API (e.g., a `sample(prompt, temperature, n)` function or class method) providing a uniform interface to the backbone LM so that Algorithm 2 (CROSSMUT) can obtain samples independently of the underlying provider.

The backbone LM interface accepts a Python-code-formatted few-shot prompt (matching Listing 1's structure) and returns raw decoded strings without additional post-processing that would alter code structure, so that outputs can be parsed as candidate `class Model` / `def get_triplet_msgs_*` blocks.

Code has been implemented that supports prompt-tuning updates to pi_theta (i.e., the backbone exposes a trainable soft-prompt parameter surface or an equivalent adapter surface) so that TRAIN(theta_t, ...) in Algorithm 1 can update pi_theta_t across rounds.
Mixed-temperature sampling from the discrete set {0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0} is implemented and exercised for every backbone LM sampling call.
Code has been implemented that defines the temperature pool exactly as the set {0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0} (e.g., as a constant list/tuple), with no other temperature values silently mixed in.

For each backbone sampling call, code selects the sampling temperature by drawing uniformly at random from {0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0} (independent draw per call), and passes the chosen temperature to the LM sampling API.

A unit test asserts that repeatedly invoking the sampling wrapper (e.g., 10,000 calls) produces an empirical distribution over the temperature set that is (approximately) uniform (each of the four values within ~5 percentage points of 25%) and never emits any temperature outside {0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0}.

The sampling wrapper logs the temperature used per candidate (recorded alongside the generated code and its evaluation) so that downstream analysis and rubric grading can verify mixed-temperature usage across a full run.
Sampling-hyperparameter integration with the CROSSMUT/EVOPROMPTING loop follows Section 4's per-round budget (10 prompts/round, 16 samples/prompt = 160 samples/round).

Code has been implemented that generates exactly n=16 samples per few-shot prompt via the backbone LM (per Section 4, Appendix A.1), by looping the sampling wrapper 16 times per prompt with independent temperature draws (or an equivalent batched call that yields 16 outputs).

Code has been implemented that issues m=10 prompts per round to the backbone LM (per Appendix A.1), yielding a total of 160 candidate samples per round from the backbone before de-duplication/filtering.

An end-to-end sanity test runs one round of CROSSMUT with the backbone LM (or a stubbed backbone honoring the same interface contract) and verifies that exactly 160 raw candidate strings are produced before duplicate/untrainable filtering.

If a substitute backbone LM is used (because 62B PaLM code-tuned is not publicly available), the substitute choice is justified, isolated, and validated against baseline behavior on the naive-few-shot task.

Code has been implemented that reads the backbone-model identity from a single configuration point (e.g., an env var or config file) so swapping the substitute for the original PaLM checkpoint (should it become available) requires no code changes to Algorithm 1/2/3.

The naive-few-shot baseline (Section 4.1) is exercised with the chosen backbone/substitute and the resulting top-20 MNIST-1D test errors are within a documented tolerance of the paper's naive-few-shot Pareto frontier (Figure 2a), demonstrating that the substitute is a credible stand-in for pi_theta_0.

Soft prompt-tuning (Lester et al. 2021) is implemented with the paper's hyperparameters: 5 epochs per round, soft prompt length 16, batch size 16, learning rate 0.1, tuned on evaluated non-selected children (C_EVALED \ P) between rounds of Algorithm 1.
The soft prompt is parameterized as a Lester et al. (2021)-style trainable prefix that is prepended to the LM's token embeddings while the base LM is frozen.
Code has been implemented that defines a soft-prompt module holding a trainable embedding table used as a prefix for prompt-tuning (Lester et al. 2021).
The soft prompt has length 16 tokens, matching the paper's specification in Section 4.
The soft-prompt embeddings have the same hidden dimensionality as the base LM's input embeddings and are prepended to the tokenized few-shot prompt when the model runs.
During prompt-tuning, only the soft-prompt parameters receive gradient updates; all backbone LM parameters are held frozen (no requires_grad / trainable=True on LM weights).
The prompt-tuning optimization procedure (TRAIN in Algorithm 1 step 11) is implemented with the paper's loss and hyperparameters.
Code has been implemented for a TRAIN(theta_t, dataset) routine that trains the soft prompt and returns updated parameters theta_{t+1}, as invoked at step 11 of Algorithm 1.
The prompt-tuning loss is the standard causal-LM next-token cross-entropy on the child architecture's code tokens (targets), conditioned on the few-shot prompt tokens plus the soft prompt.
Prompt-tuning runs for exactly 5 epochs over the round's training set per invocation, matching Section 4.
Prompt-tuning uses batch size 16, matching Section 4.
Prompt-tuning uses learning rate 0.1 (applied to the soft prompt parameters), matching Section 4.
The prompt-tuning training set is constructed from the round's evaluated non-selected children (C_EVALED \ P), matching Algorithm 1 step 11.
Code has been implemented that assembles the prompt-tuning dataset as C_EVALED minus the parents P returned by GETTOP in the current round.
Behaviorally, when GETTOP selects any subset P from C_EVALED, none of those p parent examples appear as training targets in the prompt-tuning dataset for that round.

Each prompt-tuning training example is formatted as a (few-shot prompt, child-code) pair using the same MAKEFEWSHOTPROMPT/Listing 1 formatting used at generation time, so that the tuned soft prompt is aligned with inference-time prompt structure.
Only successfully-scored children (those that passed FILTERANDEVAL and thus appear in C_EVALED) enter the prompt-tuning dataset; duplicates and un-trainable samples are excluded, matching Section 4.
The prompt-tuning module is integrated into the meta-learning loop of Algorithm 1 with correct control flow and persistence across rounds.
The end-to-end loop invokes TRAIN(theta_t, C_EVALED \ P) at step 11 of Algorithm 1, immediately after GETTOP and before incrementing t.
Behaviorally, prompt-tuning is skipped in the final round (the `if t < T - 1` guard in Algorithm 1), so exactly T-1 TRAIN calls occur across a T-round search.

The updated soft-prompt state theta_{t+1} produced by TRAIN is the one used by CROSSMUT in round t+1 (i.e. subsequent LM samples are conditioned on the tuned soft prompt, not on the previous round's prompt).
Soft-prompt parameters persist across rounds (each round's TRAIN warm-starts from theta_t rather than reinitializing), so prompt-tuning accumulates over the search.

The prompt-tuning module exposes a toggle (config flag or equivalent) that disables step 11 without altering other stages, enabling the `EvoPrompting (- prompt-tuning)` ablation reported in Section 4.1.

The end-to-end meta-learning loop of Algorithm 1 is implemented, including initialization, iteration over T rounds, GETTOP selection with permanent removal, appending children into global population G, and returning the top-p models.
The Algorithm 1 orchestration entry point exists with the correct signature and hyperparameter defaults from Section 3.3 and Table 2.

Code has been implemented that exposes a top-level `evoprompting` (or equivalently named) driver function accepting arguments matching Algorithm 1's inputs: language model pi_theta_0, dataset D, task T, T (number of rounds), m (prompts per round), n (samples per prompt), k (in-context examples per prompt), p (survivors), and alpha (upper error threshold).
Code has been implemented that supplies the default hyperparameters from Appendix Table 2: T=10, m=10, n=16, k=2, p=10, and alpha=0.5 when the caller does not override them.
The initialization stage (steps 2-4 of Algorithm 1) is implemented correctly.
Code has been implemented that initializes the global historical population `G` to an empty list at the start of the algorithm (step 2 of Algorithm 1).

Code has been implemented that calls `INITIALIZEPOPULATION(p)` to warm-start the current population `P` with the seed architectures, and evaluates the seed models with the same EVAL_T(c, D) function used for children before entering the loop.
Code has been implemented that initializes the round counter `t` to 0 before entering the while loop (step 4 of Algorithm 1).
The main meta-learning while loop (steps 5-14 of Algorithm 1) is implemented with the correct call order and control flow.
Code has been implemented that iterates exactly T rounds using a `while t < T` construct that increments `t` at the end of each iteration (matching step 13 of Algorithm 1).

Code has been implemented that, inside each round, invokes CROSSMUT(pi_theta_t, P, m, k, n) to produce the candidate set C, then invokes FILTERANDEVAL(C, T, D, alpha) to produce C_EVALED, in this exact order (steps 6-7 of Algorithm 1).

Code has been implemented that appends `C_EVALED` (list of (code, fitness) pairs surviving FILTERANDEVAL) onto the global population `G` at the end of each round (step 8 of Algorithm 1), preserving all previously evaluated members.

Code has been implemented that guards the parent-selection and prompt-tuning updates with a `if t < T - 1` check, so no selection or prompt-tuning update is performed after the last round (steps 9-12 of Algorithm 1).
GETTOP fitness-based selection with permanent removal is implemented as described in Section 3.3.
Code has been implemented that defines `GETTOP(G, p)` returning the p members of G with the highest fitness scores (where fitness = -model_size * error), ties broken deterministically.

Code has been implemented so that when a model is selected by GETTOP as a parent, it is permanently removed from `G` (or from the eligible-parents pool) and cannot be re-selected as a parent in any subsequent round, matching "they are permanently removed from the population" in Section 3.3.

GETTOP's permanent-removal behavior is exercised by a unit test that populates G with a mixture of high- and low-fitness (code, score) pairs across three simulated rounds and asserts that no code selected as a parent in an earlier round appears as a parent again.
A unit test constructs a small synthetic G with hand-set fitness scores and asserts GETTOP(G, p) returns exactly the top-p entries by fitness, matching the ordering defined in Section 3.3.
The prompt-tuning update at step 11 uses only the non-parent children as specified in Section 3.3.

Code has been implemented that computes the training set for the next-round prompt-tune as `C_EVALED \ P` (the child models generated in the current round that were not selected as parents), matching step 11 of Algorithm 1.
Code has been implemented that invokes TRAIN(theta_t, C_EVALED \ P) to produce theta_{t+1} and then uses the updated pi_theta_{t+1} for CROSSMUT in the following round.
Termination of the algorithm returns the final top-p models.

Code has been implemented so that after the T-round while loop terminates, the function returns GETTOP(G, p) — the top-p models across all evolved rounds — as the algorithm's output (step 15 of Algorithm 1).
Duplicate and untrainable candidate accounting matches Section 4 ("Duplicate models and un-trainable models are not scored, but do count into the 1600").

Code has been implemented that detects duplicate candidates (by canonicalized source-code hash across the current round and G) and skips scoring/appending them to G, while still counting them toward the per-round sample budget.

Code has been implemented that treats candidates which fail to compile/instantiate/train (un-trainable) as counted toward the n*m per-round budget but not scored and not appended to G, matching the accounting in Section 4.
Logging of per-round state supports downstream analyses (fitness trajectories, Pareto plots).

Code has been implemented that persists, per round `t`, the full C_EVALED (source, model_size, validation error, fitness), the current parent set P, and the cumulative G to disk so that Figures 2b, 3, and 4 can be regenerated without re-running the search.
Deterministic end-to-end behavior of the loop is validated by an integration test with stubbed subroutines.

An integration test drives the Algorithm 1 driver with stubbed CROSSMUT (deterministic child list), FILTERANDEVAL (deterministic scores), and TRAIN (identity), and asserts: G accumulates C_EVALED across rounds, GETTOP is not called after the final round, and the final return value equals GETTOP(G, p).
An integration test asserts that when the loop is run with T=T, the number of prompt-tune (TRAIN) invocations equals exactly T-1, verifying the `if t < T - 1` guard on step 11.
Numerical accounting claims from Section 4 about the search-scale of Algorithm 1 are reproduced.

With default hyperparameters (T=10, m=10, n=16) the driver generates exactly 160 candidate child samples per round (counting duplicates and un-trainable models), matching the "160 models generated per round" claim in Section 4.

With default hyperparameters (T=10, m=10, n=16) the entire meta-learning run generates exactly 1600 candidate child samples in total across all rounds, matching the "1600 models generated during the entire search" claim in Section 4.
The driver executes exactly 10 rounds of evolution under the default T=10 hyperparameter, and the final returned population has size exactly p=10, matching Table 2 and Section 4.

The CROSSMUT procedure (Algorithm 2) is implemented: uniform sampling of k in-context examples from the current parent population P, MAKEFEWSHOTPROMPT construction that formats each example with its metrics and appends a target-metrics header (90% of min parent size rounded to nearest 100 params, 102% of max parent val accuracy rounded to nearest 0.1%), and generation of n samples per prompt across m prompts by sampling from pi_theta with mixed temperatures, returning a concatenated list of n*m child code samples.
The top-level CROSSMUT function and its interface into the meta-learning loop are implemented.

Code has been implemented that exposes a CROSSMUT function (or method) whose signature accepts (pi_theta_t, P, m, k, n) matching Algorithm 2 line 1, and which is invoked from the meta-learning loop at step 6 of Algorithm 1.

Code has been implemented so that CROSSMUT accepts the parent population P as a set of (code, fitness) tuples where each code element is a Python string defining a neural architecture and each fitness is the scalar returned by EVAL_T.
Code has been implemented so that CROSSMUT returns a concatenated list C = C_1 + C_2 + ... + C_m of length exactly n*m child code samples (Algorithm 2 lines 8 and 11), preserving generation order.
Uniform i.i.d. sampling of k in-context examples from the parent population P is implemented as described in Algorithm 2 line 5.
Code has been implemented that samples exactly k examples per prompt from P using a uniform distribution over the parent set, matching x_j ~ Uniform(P) in Algorithm 2.

Code has been implemented so that the k in-context examples are drawn i.i.d. (independently for each of the m prompts and independently across the k slots within a prompt) rather than reusing a single shuffled list across prompts.
Over a large number of CROSSMUT calls on a fixed P, the empirical selection frequency of each parent in the in-context example slot is within +/-10% of the uniform expectation 1/|P|.
The MAKEFEWSHOTPROMPT routine that builds the few-shot prompt string in the format of Listing 1 is implemented.

Code has been implemented that exposes a MAKEFEWSHOTPROMPT(E) function which consumes a list E of k (code, metrics) parent tuples and returns a single prompt string p suitable for conditioning pi_theta.

Code has been implemented so that each in-context example in the prompt is rendered as a triple-quoted docstring block containing `Metrics:` followed by a Python dict literal with keys `num_params` and `val_accuracy`, immediately preceding the parent's `class Model(nn.Module):` source, exactly matching the format shown in Listing 1.

Code has been implemented so that the num_params value in each in-context example's Metrics block is the integer parameter count of that parent architecture and the val_accuracy value is the parent's recorded validation accuracy formatted to three decimal places, quoted as a string as shown in Listing 1.

Code has been implemented so that the prompt terminates with a final Metrics block containing the target num_params and val_accuracy but no `class Model` body, so that pi_theta is prompted to complete the class definition given the target metrics as its conditioning line.
Target-metric computation for the final prompt line (target num_params and target val_accuracy) follows the paper's exact formulas and rounding rules from Section 3.3.
Code has been implemented that computes the target model size as 0.9 * min(num_params(x) for x in E), where E is the sampled in-context example set for that prompt.
Code has been implemented so that the computed target model size is rounded to the nearest 100 parameters (e.g. 4123 -> 4100, 4750 -> 4800) before being embedded in the prompt.
Code has been implemented that computes the target validation accuracy as 1.02 * max(val_accuracy(x) for x in E), where E is the sampled in-context example set for that prompt.
Code has been implemented so that the computed target validation accuracy is rounded to the nearest 0.1% (i.e., the nearest 0.001 in decimal form) before being embedded in the prompt string.

Given a fixed synthetic parent set with num_params = [4800, 4300] and val_accuracy = [0.865, 0.880], the CROSSMUT target-line generator produces `num_params: '3900'` (0.9 * 4300 = 3870 rounded to 3900) and `val_accuracy: '0.898'` (1.02 * 0.880 = 0.8976 rounded to 0.898) to within the rounding rules above.
Sampling n child code samples per prompt across m prompts via pi_theta is implemented per Algorithm 2 lines 4-10.

Code has been implemented that iterates the outer loop m times (Algorithm 2 line 4) and for each iteration builds one few-shot prompt via MAKEFEWSHOTPROMPT and generates n i.i.d. completions c_j ~ pi_theta(. | p) that are collected into C_i.

Code has been implemented that requests exactly n completions from the language model per prompt (either via a single call with num_samples=n or n separate decode calls with independent seeds), so that after m prompts the returned C has exactly n*m entries.

Code has been implemented that applies mixed-temperature sampling by drawing the decoding temperature uniformly at random from the set {0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0} for each generation, as specified in Section 4.
For a CROSSMUT invocation with m=10 and n=16 the returned child list contains exactly 160 code samples, matching Section 4's statement that 160 models are generated per round.
The paper's default CROSSMUT hyperparameter values (Table 2) are wired through as defaults or configuration.
Code has been implemented so that k defaults to 2 (in-context examples per prompt), matching Listing 1 and Table 2.
Code has been implemented so that m defaults to 10 prompts per round of evolution, matching Table 2.
Code has been implemented so that n defaults to 16 samples generated per prompt, matching Table 2.

The FILTERANDEVAL routine (Algorithm 3) is implemented to train each candidate child model, compute a validation error, filter by upper error threshold alpha, compute fitness as -(model_size * error), and correctly handle duplicates and un-trainable models by skipping scoring while still counting them toward the sample budget.
The FILTERANDEVAL function is defined with the correct signature and return contract as specified in Algorithm 3.
Code has been implemented that exposes a FILTERANDEVAL (or equivalently named) function in the EvoPrompting method module, importable from the search package.
Code has been implemented so that FILTERANDEVAL accepts the four inputs specified in Algorithm 3: a set of code samples C, a task T, a dataset D, and an upper error threshold alpha.
Code has been implemented so that FILTERANDEVAL returns C_EVALED as a list of (code_sample, fitness_score) pairs, matching the output contract in Algorithm 3.
The per-child evaluation function EVAL_T is implemented to train candidate architectures and return a validation error.
Code has been implemented for EVAL_T that trains the child model encoded by code c on dataset D and returns a real-valued validation error, matching step 4 of Algorithm 3.

Code has been implemented so that EVAL_T records the lowest validation error encountered during training and returns that value (per Section 3.3, 'returns the lowest validation error encountered during training').

Code has been implemented so that all child models within a FILTERANDEVAL call are trained for the same fixed number of steps and with identical optimizer hyperparameters (per Section 3.3, 'All child models are trained for the same number of steps, with the same optimizer hyperparameters').
Code has been implemented so that the error attribute (c.error) of each candidate is set from EVAL_T's return value before threshold filtering is applied, per Algorithm 3 step 4.
Error-threshold filtering by alpha is implemented as specified in Algorithm 3 step 5.
Code has been implemented so that a candidate is retained only when c.error < alpha (strict less-than comparison), matching the conditional in step 5 of Algorithm 3.
Code has been implemented so that candidates with c.error >= alpha are excluded from C_EVALED (they are not added to the global population G with a fitness score).
The default value of the upper error threshold alpha used in EvoPrompting is 0.5, matching the value reported in Appendix A.1 Table 2.
Fitness scoring is implemented as the negative product of model size and validation error per step 6 of Algorithm 3.
Code has been implemented so the fitness score is computed exactly as s = -(c.model_size * c.error), matching step 6 of Algorithm 3.
Code has been implemented that derives c.model_size from the child model's total trainable parameter count (num_params), as used in the target-metric prompt line (Listing 1).
For two children with equal error but different sizes, the smaller model receives a strictly larger (less negative) fitness score in the implemented scoring routine.
Duplicate and un-trainable child models are handled so that they are not scored but still count toward the per-round sample budget (Section 4).
Code has been implemented that detects duplicate candidate architectures (e.g. by source-code normalization or hashing) prior to scoring, so duplicates are not added to C_EVALED.

Code has been implemented that catches un-trainable child models (compile/import/runtime errors during EVAL_T) without crashing the loop, marking them as un-trainable rather than adding them to C_EVALED.

Code has been implemented so that duplicate and un-trainable models are still counted against the m*n per-round sample budget and the overall 1600-sample search budget (per Section 4: 'Duplicate models and un-trainable models are not scored, but do count into the 1600').
FILTERANDEVAL integrates with the outer meta-learning loop by appending scored children to the global population G.
Code has been implemented so C_EVALED as returned by FILTERANDEVAL is concatenated onto the global historical population G in the outer loop (Algorithm 1 step 8), preserving (code, fitness) pairs.

A unit-level test exercises FILTERANDEVAL on a small hand-crafted set of candidates and verifies that (a) candidates above alpha are excluded, (b) accepted candidates carry fitness = -(model_size * error), and (c) duplicates and untrainable stubs are excluded from output but still increment a per-round evaluation counter.

The MNIST-1D dataset (Greydanus 2020) is prepared with the paper's splits (4000 train, 500 held-out validation from the training set, 1000 test, 40-dimensional examples), and the four Flax seed models (GRU, CNN baseline, MLP, and larger custom CNN) are implemented per Appendix A.2.
The MNIST-1D dataset is loaded/generated with the paper's exact structure and split sizes.
Code has been implemented that downloads or generates the MNIST-1D dataset from the Greydanus (2020) source (e.g., the mnist1d pickle / generator) and exposes it as train/test arrays for the search.
The loaded MNIST-1D examples are 40-dimensional 1D signals (input feature dimension exactly 40) as described in Section 4.1.
The prepared training set contains exactly 4000 examples and the prepared test set contains exactly 1000 examples, matching the counts stated in Section 4.1.
Code has been implemented that randomly sets aside exactly 500 examples from the 4000-example training set as a held-out validation set (leaving 3500 for training), as described in Section 4.1.
The validation-split routine is deterministic under a fixed seed so that repeated invocations yield the same 500-example validation subset, enabling reproducible fitness scoring.
The dataset loader exposes labels as integers in {0, ..., 9} corresponding to 10 classes, matching the classification target used by the seed models' 10-unit output layer.
The four Flax seed models from Appendix A.2 (Listings 2-5) are implemented so that they can be used as warm-start parents in the MNIST-1D search.

The larger custom CNN seed model (Listing 2) is implemented as a Flax nn.Module with features=32 and nlayer=3 defaults, an initial Conv(features=32, kernel_size=(3,)) followed by ReLU and avg_pool(window=(2,), strides=(2,)), then nlayer-1 residual Conv(features=32, kernel_size=(3,))+ReLU blocks, a final avg_pool, a flatten, a Dense(256)+ReLU, and a final Dense(10).

The CNN baseline seed model (Listing 3) is implemented as a Flax nn.Module with features=25, a first Conv(features=25, kernel_size=(5,), strides=(2,), padding=(1,))+ReLU, then two Conv(features=25, kernel_size=(3,), strides=(2,), padding=(1,))+ReLU blocks, a flatten, and a final Dense(10).

The GRU seed model (Listing 4) is implemented as a Flax nn.Module with hidden_size=6 default, a bidirectional single-layer GRU with dropout_rate=0.0 applied over the 40-dim sequence (with lengths=40 per example), followed by a flatten and a Dense(10) output layer.

The MLP seed model (Listing 5) is implemented as a Flax nn.Module with hidden_size=100 default, an initial Dense(100)+ReLU, one residual block of the form x = x + ReLU(Dense(100)(x)), and a final Dense(10) output layer.
All four seed models are implemented using the Flax linen API (nn.Module with @nn.compact __call__) so they are compatible with the Flax training loop used by FILTERANDEVAL.
The seed models and dataset are wired together so that each seed model runs end-to-end on MNIST-1D inputs and is exposed to the search as an initial parent.

Each of the four seed models, when instantiated with default hyperparameters, accepts a batch of MNIST-1D inputs of shape (batch, 40) (with the CNN models internally adding a trailing channel dim via x[..., None]) and returns logits of shape (batch, 10) without raising a shape or dtype error.

Code has been implemented to compute each seed model's num_params (trainable parameter count) so that these values can be attached to the seed entries in the initial population P and used to construct the target-metrics prompt line.

INITIALIZEPOPULATION(p) for the MNIST-1D task returns a population containing exactly the four seed models (GRU, CNN baseline, MLP, larger custom CNN from Listings 2-5) as the warm-start parents, matching Section 4.1's statement that the search is seeded with 4 seed models.

Each seed model can be trained for a smoke-test number of AdamW steps on the 3500/500/1000 MNIST-1D split and produces a validation accuracy strictly above 0.10 (i.e., meaningfully better than random guessing over 10 classes), confirming the seeds are functional warm-starts.
The seed models achieve validation accuracies consistent with the hand-designed baselines reported by Greydanus (2020) / used as warm-starts by EvoPrompting.
